paragraphs.text: Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic, said on Friday, November 20, 2026, that he had found a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis while working with the company's Claude model. In a four-page note, he wrote that he believes he discovered the proof working with Claude, according to AFP. He also said the method resolves a broader version of the problem known as the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis.

The Riemann Hypothesis was first proposed by the German mathematician Bernhard Riemann in 1859. It concerns how prime numbers are distributed and is widely regarded as the most important open question in pure mathematics, AFP reported. It is one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems chosen by the Clay Mathematics Institute in 2000, each carrying a $1 million award.
A proof written for a computer

Alpöge did not release a conventional written paper. According to AFP, he said he and Claude produced a version of the proof in Lean, a programming language that lets a computer check mathematical arguments step by step, and that he was releasing only that version for now. He said a full written argument would be extremely long, that he had not yet mastered all of the mathematics involved, and that he planned to write it up properly.

Kingy AI downloaded the published archive and reported that it came in 14 parts totaling about 239 million bytes, with 175,187 Lean source files. The outlet said it read the top level theorem files but did not compile or replay the proof itself. It also noted that an independent verification project had so far compiled only the stated challenge against Mathlib, the shared Lean math library, while a full check was still running.

In Alpöge's own account, as described by Kingy AI, he directed the investigation toward a setting suggested by ideas from a simpler model and credits Claude with rapid progress near the end. The announcement does not name a specific Claude model.
Not verified, and not yet eligible for the prize

AFP reported that the claim has not been independently verified and that outside experts have not yet reviewed the proof. Under the Clay Institute's rules, a solution must be published in a peer reviewed journal and withstand two years of scrutiny before the prize can be awarded. Kingy AI said the institute's Riemann page still listed the problem as unsolved on November 20.

Alpöge consulted Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei before announcing the result and acknowledged that its timing could be viewed cynically, AFP said, likely a reference to Anthropic's record IPO earlier the same week. Anthropic did not immediately respond to AFP's request for comment.

The claim follows earlier work on the same problem. In August, Anthropic said an unreleased version of Claude had improved a long standing result related to the Riemann Hypothesis while stressing that it had not proved it. Kingy AI described that result as showing at least 67.25 percent of the nontrivial zeros of the zeta function lie on the critical line. AFP also noted that OpenAI said two months ago that an AI model had solved another Millennium Prize Problem, on the equations that govern fluid motion.

A machine-checkable proof changes how quickly a claim like this can be tested. If the Lean code compiles and the formal statement matches the real hypothesis, the remaining doubt narrows to whether the statement was encoded correctly, which is a question specialists can answer far faster than reading a long human proof line by line.

The next signal to watch is whether independent teams finish compiling the full Lean archive and whether number theorists confirm that its formal statement is the Riemann Hypothesis as mathematicians understand it.
